CALIFORNIA FAIR PAY ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS CALIFORNIA FAIR PAY ACT INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes selected requirements of California Labor Code section 1197.5, sometimes referred to as California's Fair Pay Act or Equal Pay Act, as it may relate to compensation paid by Acme, Inc. to Jordan Lee in connection with the position of Software Engineer. Section 1197.5 addresses pay comparisons based on sex and, separately, on race or ethnicity, the specific factors an employer may rely on to justify a pay differential, protections against retaliation for invoking or assisting in the enforcement of the section, and a wage-and-job-classification recordkeeping duty. This document is California-specific: it describes only what this one California statute says. It is not a determination that any wage rate paid or not paid by Acme, Inc. to Jordan Lee, or to any other employee, complies or fails to comply with section 1197.5, and it does not itself satisfy any recordkeeping, notice, or reporting duty the statute may impose.

THE CORE PROHIBITION: SEX-BASED AND RACE/ETHNICITY-BASED PAY DIFFERENTIALS FOR SUBSTANTIALLY SIMILAR WORK
California Labor Code section 1197.5 states its core prohibition in two separate, parallel subdivisions rather than a single unified provision. Subdivision (a) prohibits an employer from paying any of its employees at wage rates less than the rates paid to employees of another sex for substantially similar work, when viewed as a composite of skill, effort, and responsibility, and performed under similar working conditions, unless the employer demonstrates specified factors. Subdivision (b), using materially identical wording, separately prohibits paying any of its employees at wage rates less than the rates paid to employees of another race or ethnicity for substantially similar work, viewed and performed under the same composite standard, unless the employer demonstrates the same kind of factors. The comparison standard in both subdivisions is "substantially similar work," assessed as a composite of skill, effort, and responsibility performed under similar working conditions — not a requirement that the compared jobs be identical.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "An employer shall not pay any of its employees at wage rates less than the rates paid to employees of another sex for substantially similar work, when viewed as a composite of skill, effort, and responsibility, and performed under similar working conditions, except where the employer demonstrates:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, sex-based equal-pay prohibition and comparison standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "An employer shall not pay any of its employees at wage rates less than the rates paid to employees of another race or ethnicity for substantially similar work, when viewed as a composite of skill, effort, and responsibility, and performed under similar working conditions, except where the employer demonstrates:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, race- and ethnicity-based equal-pay prohibition and comparison standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(a) and (b)), used as real evidence of the statute's core prohibition and its comparison standard — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The two citations below are to subdivisions (a) and (b) of a single statutory section; they are not independent sources of each other, since subdivision (b) was evidently drafted as a parallel to subdivision (a) and both were confirmed from the same two fetches of the same section. This section was last amended effective January 1, 2026 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 468 (SB 642)); this clause reflects the section's currently codified text as fetched on the date below, not any prior or superseded version. Section 1197.5's own text does not define "substantially similar work" beyond the composite-factors language quoted here, and this clause does not determine whether any two specific positions, or the work actually performed in them, are or are not substantially similar within the meaning of the statute.

THE AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE: ENUMERATED BONA FIDE FACTORS, AND THE LIMIT ON PRIOR SALARY
Section 1197.5 does not prohibit every pay differential between employees of different sexes, races, or ethnicities doing substantially similar work; it makes the prohibition subject to an affirmative defense the employer bears the burden of demonstrating. Under subdivision (a) (and, in parallel, subdivision (b) for race and ethnicity), the wage differential must be based upon one or more of a specific, enumerated list of factors: a seniority system; a merit system; a system that measures earnings by quantity or quality of production; or a bona fide factor other than sex (or, under subdivision (b), other than race or ethnicity), such as education, training, or experience. That last, catch-all factor is itself conditioned: it applies only if the employer demonstrates the factor is not based on or derived from a sex-based (or race- or ethnicity-based) differential in compensation, is job related to the position in question, and is consistent with a "business necessity," which the statute defines as an overriding legitimate business purpose that the factor effectively fulfills; even then, the catch-all defense does not apply if the employee demonstrates an alternative business practice exists that would serve the same business purpose without producing the wage differential. Beyond identifying a qualifying factor, the statute imposes two further requirements: each factor relied upon must be applied reasonably, and the factor or factors relied upon must account for the entire wage differential, not merely part of it. Separately, the statute states that prior salary shall not justify any disparity in compensation, while clarifying that this does not prevent an employer from basing a compensation decision on a current employee's existing salary, so long as any resulting wage differential is itself justified by one or more of the enumerated factors.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(1) The wage differential is based upon one or more of the following factors: (A) A seniority system. (B) A merit system. (C) A system that measures earnings by quantity or quality of production."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a)(1)(A)-(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, seniority system, merit system, and quantity/quality-of-production factors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "(D) A bona fide factor other than sex, such as education, training, or experience. This factor shall apply only if the employer demonstrates that the factor is not based on or derived from a sex-based differential in compensation, is job related with respect to the position in question, and is consistent with a business necessity."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a)(1)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, catch-all bona fide factor and its job-relatedness/business-necessity conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "For purposes of this subparagraph, “business necessity” means an overriding legitimate business purpose such that the factor relied upon effectively fulfills the business purpose it is supposed to serve. This defense shall not apply if the employee demonstrates that an alternative business practice exists that would serve the same business purpose without producing the wage differential."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a)(1)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, statutory definition of "business necessity" and the alternative-business-practice rebuttal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "(2) Each factor relied upon is applied reasonably. (3) The one or more factors relied upon account for the entire wage differential."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a)(2)-(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, reasonable-application and entire-differential requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "(4) Prior salary shall not justify any disparity in compensation. Nothing in this section shall be interpreted to mean that an employer may not make a compensation decision based on a current employee’s existing salary, so long as any wage differential resulting from that compensation decision is justified by one or more of the factors in this subdivision."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, prior-salary limitation and existing-salary clarification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(a)(1) through (a)(4), and the parallel language in (b)(1) through (b)(4)), used as real evidence of the statute's affirmative-defense structure — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any specific pay differential is or is not justified. The citations below are all to subparagraphs of subdivision (a) of a single statutory section; subdivision (b) restates the same structure with "race or ethnicity" substituted for "sex" and is not cited separately as an independent source, since it is textually parallel rather than independently corroborating. This clause does not resolve, and the statute's text does not itself specify, how much of a wage differential must be "accounted for" before a factor is treated as covering the "entire" differential in a case involving more than one factor, nor does it identify any particular alternative-business-practice showing that would or would not defeat the catch-all factor in a specific case; this clause does not identify any reported court decision applying these factors to particular facts, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption.

REMEDIES FOR A VIOLATION AND THE STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS
Section 1197.5 states that an employer who violates the sex-based prohibition in subdivision (a) or the race/ethnicity-based prohibition in subdivision (b) is liable to the affected employee for the amount of wages and interest of which the employee was deprived, plus an additional equal amount as liquidated damages. Consistent with this, an employee receiving less than the wage to which the employee is entitled may recover the balance of the wages, including interest, an equal amount as liquidated damages, and the costs of suit and reasonable attorney's fees, in a civil action, and this remedy applies notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage. The statute sets its own limitations period for this kind of civil action: a civil action to recover wages under subdivision (a) or (b) must be commenced no later than three years after the last date the cause of action occurs, while the employee's entitlement to relief for a continuing violation can reach back for the entire period the violation existed, up to a maximum of six years.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Any employer who violates subdivision (a) or (b) is liable to the employee affected in the amount of the wages, and interest thereon, of which the employee is deprived by reason of the violation, and an additional equal amount as liquidated damages."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employer liability for wages, interest, and liquidated damages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "An employee receiving less than the wage to which the employee is entitled under this section may recover in a civil action the balance of the wages, including interest thereon, and an equal amount as liquidated damages, together with the costs of the suit and reasonable attorney’s fees, notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, private civil action for unpaid wages, liquidated damages, and attorney's fees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "(1) A civil action to recover wages under subdivision (a) or (b) may be commenced no later than three years after the last date the cause of action occurs."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(i)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, three-year period to commence a civil action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "(2) An employee is entitled to obtain relief for the entire period of time in which a violation of subdivision (a) or (b) exists, but not to exceed six years."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(i)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, six-year cap on the period of relief for a continuing violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(c), (h), (i)(1), and (i)(2)), used as real evidence of the statute's remedies and limitations period — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular employee is entitled to any particular recovery. The four citations below are all to subdivisions of a single statutory section and are treated as one source describing one connected remedial scheme, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause does not restate subdivision (i)(3)'s definitions of when a cause of action "occurs," subdivision (i)(4)'s preservation of the continuing-violation and discovery-rule doctrines, subdivision (d)'s administrative enforcement track through the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, subdivision (g)'s provision for a civil action brought by the department or division itself, or subdivision (j)'s offset against a related federal Equal Pay Act recovery; a reader consulting the statute's full text will find additional remedial and procedural detail beyond what this clause summarizes. This clause does not identify any reported court decision applying these remedies or this limitations period to particular facts, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption.

RECORDKEEPING DUTY AND ADMINISTRATIVE ENFORCEMENT BY THE DIVISION OF LABOR STANDARDS ENFORCEMENT
Section 1197.5 requires every employer to maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of the persons it employs, and requires those records to be kept on file for a period of three years. The statute assigns administrative responsibility for the section to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, which the statute directs to administer and enforce the section, including by investigating an employee's complaint that wages paid are less than the wages to which the employee is entitled, or that the employer has violated the anti-retaliation subdivision. In connection with a complaint alleging a violation of the sex-based prohibition, the race/ethnicity-based prohibition, or the anti-retaliation provision, the statute directs the Division to keep confidential the name of the complaining employee until the Division establishes the validity of the complaint, unless confidentiality must be abridged to investigate, and states that the name remains confidential if the complaint is withdrawn before that point.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement shall administer and enforce this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Division of Labor Standards Enforcement administers and enforces the section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "Every employer shall maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of the persons employed by the employer. All of the records shall be kept on file for a period of three years."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, wage, wage-rate, and job-classification recordkeeping duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "The division shall keep confidential the name of any employee who submits to the division a complaint regarding an alleged violation of subdivision (a), (b), or (k) until the division establishes the validity of the complaint, unless the division must abridge confidentiality to investigate the complaint."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, confidentiality of a complaining employee's name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(d), (e), and (f)), used as real evidence of the recordkeeping duty and the administrative enforcement and confidentiality framework — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The three citations below are to subdivisions of a single statutory section and are treated as one source describing one connected recordkeeping-and-enforcement scheme, not as independent corroborating sources; this recordkeeping duty and its three-year retention period are also cited, from the same subdivision (e), in a separate clause of a different information sheet in this corpus addressing Labor Code section 432.3, disclosed here rather than presented as a newly discovered source. This clause does not restate the full text of subdivision (f)'s complaint-investigation cross-reference to Labor Code section 98.7(b), and does not determine that any particular employer has or has not maintained the required records for any particular employee, or that the Division has or would find any particular complaint valid. This clause is informational only.

ANTI-RETALIATION PROVISION AND THE PROTECTED RIGHT TO DISCUSS WAGES
Section 1197.5 includes its own anti-retaliation provision, separate from the general prohibition on unequal pay. It states that an employer shall not discharge, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against, an employee by reason of any action the employee takes to invoke or assist in enforcing the section, and that if an employer takes a prohibited action within 90 days of the employee's protected activity, a rebuttable presumption arises in favor of the employee's claim. Within this same provision, the statute separately protects pay-transparency-related conduct: an employer shall not prohibit an employee from disclosing the employee's own wages, discussing the wages of others, inquiring about another employee's wages, or aiding or encouraging another employee to exercise rights under the section, though the statute is explicit that this does not itself create any obligation to disclose wages. An employee who has been discharged, discriminated, or retaliated against in violation of this provision may recover, in a civil action, reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, including interest, as well as appropriate equitable relief; such an action must be commenced no later than one year after the cause of action occurs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "An employer shall not discharge, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against, any employee by reason of any action taken by the employee to invoke or assist in any manner the enforcement of this section. If an employer engages in any action prohibited by this section within 90 days of the protected activity specified in this section, there shall be a rebuttable presumption in favor of the employee’s claim."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(k)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, anti-retaliation prohibition and 90-day rebuttable presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "An employer shall not prohibit an employee from disclosing the employee’s own wages, discussing the wages of others, inquiring about another employee’s wages, or aiding or encouraging any other employee to exercise their rights under this section. Nothing in this section creates an obligation to disclose wages."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(k)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, protection for disclosing or discussing wages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "Any employee who has been discharged, discriminated or retaliated against, in the terms and conditions of their employment because the employee engaged in any conduct delineated in this section may recover in a civil action reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer, including interest thereon, as well as appropriate equitable relief."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(k)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, civil remedy of reinstatement and reimbursement for retaliation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  "(3) A civil action brought under this subdivision may be commenced no later than one year after the cause of action occurs."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.5(k)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, one-year statute of limitations for a retaliation action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(k)(1) through (k)(3)), used as real evidence of the section's anti-retaliation and wage-discussion provisions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The citations below are all to paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision, (k), and are treated as one source, not as independent corroborating sources; the 90-day rebuttable-presumption language and the wage-discussion protection are both drawn from the same paragraph, (k)(1), and are not independent of each other either. This clause does not determine that any particular employer action taken toward any particular employee was or was not "by reason of" protected activity within the meaning of subdivision (k)(1), does not determine that any particular 90-day window applies to any particular set of facts, and does not identify any reported court decision applying this provision to particular facts, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. This clause is informational only.

expectedJSON.body: Section 1197.5 requires every employer to maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of the persons it employs, and requires those records to be kept on file for a period of three years. The statute assigns administrative responsibility for the section to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, which the statute directs to administer and enforce the section, including by investigating an employee's complaint that wages paid are less than the wages to which the employee is entitled, or that the employer has violated the anti-retaliation subdivision. In connection with a complaint alleging a violation of the sex-based prohibition, the race/ethnicity-based prohibition, or the anti-retaliation provision, the statute directs the Division to keep confidential the name of the complaining employee until the Division establishes the validity of the complaint, unless confidentiality must be abridged to investigate, and states that the name remains confidential if the complaint is withdrawn before that point.

expectedJSON.body: Section 1197.5 includes its own anti-retaliation provision, separate from the general prohibition on unequal pay. It states that an employer shall not discharge, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against, an employee by reason of any action the employee takes to invoke or assist in enforcing the section, and that if an employer takes a prohibited action within 90 days of the employee's protected activity, a rebuttable presumption arises in favor of the employee's claim. Within this same provision, the statute separately protects pay-transparency-related conduct: an employer shall not prohibit an employee from disclosing the employee's own wages, discussing the wages of others, inquiring about another employee's wages, or aiding or encouraging another employee to exercise rights under the section, though the statute is explicit that this does not itself create any obligation to disclose wages. An employee who has been discharged, discriminated, or retaliated against in violation of this provision may recover, in a civil action, reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, including interest, as well as appropriate equitable relief; such an action must be commenced no later than one year after the cause of action occurs.
